en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-siṃhavikrīḍita-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, translator unknown, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at the palace of the Dragon King on the banks of the great lake Anavatapta.
He was accompanied by a community of five hundred great bhikṣus and a multitude of one thousand great bodhisattvas,
all of whom had attained dhāraṇīs.
Abiding in the tenth stage, one is destined to succeed to the position of the Honored One;
in a single lifetime, one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieve unimpeded penetration into all realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Adorned with the great adornments,
his mind was free from doubt or obstruction regarding the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva.
Named Siṃhavikrīḍita,
he came and took his seat in the assembly;
immediately rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes.
Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee on the ground,
he joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings..."
"How much merit does one obtain by making offerings to the Buddha with a mind of reverence and faith?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin, saying:
"Good son, do not speak such words."
Why is this? If one considers the mass of merit from making offerings to the Buddha, it is immeasurable and boundless. Why is that?

Because the Tathāgata has accomplished the immeasurable body of morality, the body of concentration, the body of wisdom, the body of liberation, and the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he is like a lion’s spring;
if there are sentient beings who behold the All-Knowing One, [they shall attain liberation].
With pure faith, they made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise;
they bestowed all that is necessary for well-being—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites for the maintenance of the body.
By making such offerings as these in the present,
and if there should be another person who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, makes an offering to his relics even as small as a mustard seed—
the merit of these two persons is exactly equal and without distinction.
Furthermore, Siṃhavikrīḍita,
if there is a lay bodhisattva who possesses a heap of the seven precious jewels as vast as Mount Sumeru.
While those who follow the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as other renunciants practicing the path,
may make offerings, one who possesses the bodhicitta may give even a single small coin as an act of almsgiving.
This merit surpasses the former by a hundredfold, a thousandfold,
a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, and even by an incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* fold;
it cannot be reached by calculation, analogy, or metaphor.
Furthermore, Siṃhavikrīḍita,
suppose there were sentient beings who, for a hundred thousand years,
made offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with every kind of article of pleasure present before him.
Furthermore, if there is another person who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
offers even a single flower to the Tathāgata,
or sweeps and sprinkles the Buddha’s stūpa, or smears and repairs the ground of the stūpa.
They burned incense, lit lamps, and offered banners, canopies, and music as an offering to the Buddha,
saying these words:
"Namo Buddhāya."
Having fully practiced asceticism for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
he accumulated all merits and attained equal and perfect enlightenment,
benefiting and bringing accomplishment to immeasurable sentient beings.
If one can thus give rise to a sincere mind to make offerings to the Buddha,
that person will not fall into the evil realms for a subsequent eon, a hundred eons, or even ten million eons.
Furthermore, Siṃhavikrīḍita,
there is a dhāraṇī called Puṣpasaṃcaya.
I now [teach it] for the sake of benefiting, bringing peace and happiness to, and enriching many sentient beings.
Out of compassion for the world, for the benefit and peace of devas and humans,
I shall now proclaim it.
O Siṃhavikrīḍita, if there be anyone who receives and upholds this Puṣpakūṭa Dhāraṇī, [they shall attain these benefits].
Such a person will constantly attain the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives;
hereafter, they shall never fall into the three evil realms,
will be born in places free from hardship, and shall not be separated from the Three Jewels.
They shall never be born into lowly families and shall never cease recollecting the Buddha.
In all places where they take birth, their faculties shall be unimpaired,
and in every life they shall not lose the mind of enlightenment.
They will attain various kinds of profound eloquence and constantly behold incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One then spoke this dhāraṇī.

If there are those who hear the name of this Flower Cluster Dhāraṇī and,
with pure faith, recollect, chant, and uphold it,
desiring to practice it.
It should be practiced during the second, third, or eighth month.
Beginning from the eighth day of the month until the fifteenth day,
one should recollect the Buddha with a single mind during three periods of the day and three periods of the night.
By making offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and light to the Triple Gem,
one will, on the fifteenth day,
behold all the Buddhas seated upon lotus thrones expounding the Dharma.
Having attained dhāraṇī, their mindfulness shall be firm and their resolve clear;
from this point until they reach bodhi,
they shall remember and retain everything they hear without ever forgetting it.
Regarding all scriptures, crafts, and arts, as well as all samādhis,
the mind attains purity upon seeing the Four Truths. Why is this?
Because this dharma is comprised within the untainted (anāsrava),
when this dharma was being taught,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita—
The bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, devas, nāgas,
yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, and non-humans,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāḍita (The Lion’s Valiant Stride)
